learner:
Beginner-intermediate guitarist who plays by ear and knows open and some barre chords. Cannot read notation, so all examples use frets and note names.
Goal: understand enough theory to write original chord progressions.
Knows the notes of C major. Correctly guessed that a key has seven chords.
Gap: does not know what makes a chord minor. Has no interval vocabulary yet.

lessons.title: Half Steps and Whole Steps on the Fretboard
lessons.objective: Measure distances between notes in half steps and whole steps using frets.
lessons.hook: Every scale and chord is built from these two distances.
lessons.explain: A half step is the distance of one fret on guitar. A whole step equals two half steps, or two frets. Most natural notes are a whole step apart, so C to D skips C#. But E to F and B to C are half steps, with no note between them. There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats at the octave. Example: on the A string, fret 0 is A, fret 2 is B, and fret 3 is C.
key_facts: A half step is the distance of one fret on guitar.
A whole step equals two half steps, or two frets.
E to F and B to C are half steps, with no note between them.
There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats at the octave.

predict.q: On the A string, which note is at fret 3?

angles: Picture a piano. Black keys sit between most pairs of white keys, but two pairs of white keys have no black key between them. Moving from any key to the very next key, black or white, is the smallest possible step.
Think of the frets as rungs on a ladder. Each rung is the smallest move, and a bigger move skips one rung. Find the note one rung above the open low E string by ear.
claims: One fret equals one half step.
A whole step is two half steps.
E–F and B–C have no note between them.
There are 12 distinct pitch classes in an octave.

items.q: How many frets make a whole step?
items.why: A whole step is two half steps, and each half step is one fret.
misconceptions: Thinks a whole step is one fret
Confuses a whole step with a minor third
Confuses a whole step with a major third

items.q: Which pair of notes is only a half step apart?
items.why: E to F has no note between them, so it is a half step.
misconceptions: Thinks all neighboring letters are a half step apart
Thinks all neighboring letters are a half step apart
Thinks all neighboring letters are a half step apart

items.q: Moving from fret 5 to fret 6 on any string is a...
items.why: One fret is one half step.

items.why: The 7 natural notes plus 5 sharps or flats make 12.
misconceptions: Counts only the natural notes

items.q: Name the two pairs of natural notes that have no sharp or flat between them.
accept: E to F and B to C
items.why: These are the only natural half steps.

items.q: You play the open A string. Which fret gives the note a whole step above A, and what is that note?
items.why: A whole step is two frets, and the next letter after A is B.

lessons.title: The Major Scale Formula
lessons.objective: Build any major scale with the step pattern.
lessons.hook: The major scale is the raw material for every chord in a key.
lessons.explain: The major scale follows the step pattern W W H W W W H. The scale starts and ends on its root note, called the tonic. From C, the pattern lands only on natural notes: C D E F G A B C. Applying the pattern from G gives G A B C D E F#. Because E to F is only a half step, the F must be raised to F#. A major scale uses each letter name exactly once. On one string, the scale falls on frets 0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 12.
key_facts: The major scale follows the step pattern W W H W W W H.
The scale starts and ends on its root note, called the tonic.
Applying the pattern from G gives G A B C D E F#.
A major scale uses each letter name exactly once.

predict.q: If you start on G and follow the major pattern, what is the seventh note?

angles: On one string, play 'Do Re Mi' up to the next 'Do' by ear. Mark the two spots where neighboring notes are only one fret apart, then write out the gaps yourself.
Build F major one step at a time. When you reach the fourth note, the pitch sits between A and B. Check which letters you have already used to decide how to spell it.

rungs.text: Build D major. Start on D. W→E, W→F#, H→G, W→A, W→B, W→C#, H→D. Result: D E F# G A B C#.
Build A major. Start on A. W→B, W→C#, H→__, W→E, W→__, W→G#, H→A.
Build E major with the step pattern, using each letter name once.

claims: The major scale pattern is W W H W W W H.
G major contains F#.
Each letter appears once in a major scale.

lessons.title: Intervals: Thirds and Fifths
lessons.objective: Identify major thirds, minor thirds, and perfect fifths by counting half steps.
lessons.explain: An interval is the distance between two notes. Intervals are measured in half steps, or frets. A major third spans 4 half steps, as in C to E. A minor third spans 3 half steps, as in C to E♭ or A to C. A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps, as in C to G. On guitar, C is at the 3rd fret of the A string. The E a major third above it is 4 frets higher, at the 7th fret of the same string.
key_facts: An interval is the distance between two notes.
A major third spans 4 half steps.
A minor third spans 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps.
angles: Count frets out loud from your starting note, calling it zero. Try counting from G up to B, then from G up to B♭, and compare the two totals.
Think of a ruler marked in frets. An interval's name depends only on how many marks you pass, not on which string you play it on.
claims: A major third is 4 half steps.
A minor third is 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth is 7 half steps.
C to E is a major third.
A to C is a minor third.

items.q: How many half steps are in a major third?
items.why: A major third spans 4 half steps.
misconceptions: Confuses a major third with a whole step
Confuses a major third with a minor third
Confuses a major third with a perfect fourth

items.q: Which pair of notes forms a minor third?
items.why: A to C spans 3 half steps.
misconceptions: Thinks C to E is a minor third
Confuses a fifth with a third
Confuses a whole step with a third

items.q: What interval is C to G?
items.why: C to G spans 7 half steps.
misconceptions: Counts letters wrongly
Counts letters wrongly
Miscounts the half steps

items.q: What is an interval?
options: The first note of a scale
items.why: This is the definition of an interval.
misconceptions: Confuses an interval with a triad
Confuses an interval with tempo
Confuses an interval with the tonic

items.q: How many half steps are in a perfect fifth?
items.why: A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps.

items.q: Which note is a major third above D?
items.why: Counting 4 half steps up from D lands on F#.

lessons.title: What Makes a Chord Major or Minor
lessons.objective: Spell major and minor triads and explain how they differ.
lessons.hook: One note decides whether a chord sounds bright or dark.
lessons.explain: A triad is three notes: root, third, and fifth. The third decides the chord's quality. A major triad has a major third above the root, so C major is C E G. A minor triad has a minor third above the root, so C minor is C E♭ G. Major and minor triads share the same perfect fifth. Compare open E (E G# B) with open Em (E G B). Lifting one finger lowers G# to G, which turns the major chord into a minor one.
key_facts: A triad is three notes: root, third, and fifth.
A major triad has a major third above the root.
A minor triad has a minor third above the root.
Major and minor triads share the same perfect fifth.
fixes: Did not know what makes a chord minor

predict.q: Open E and open Em differ by one finger. Which chord note changes?

angles: Play open A, then open Am. Watch which finger moves and by how many frets, then work out which of the three chord tones that finger was holding.
Think of the root and fifth as a fixed frame and the middle note as a mood switch. Measure how far the switch sits from the root in frets.
claims: A triad has a root, third, and fifth.
A minor triad has a minor third above the root.
C major is C E G.
C minor is C E♭ G.
Open E contains G#, and open Em contains G.

items.q: What makes a chord minor?
options: A minor third above the root
A lowered fifth above the root
A sad lyric over the chord
Playing it on the lower strings
items.answer: A minor third above the root
items.why: Chord quality is set by the third.
misconceptions: Confuses minor with diminished
Thinks minor is about mood, not notes
Thinks the register sets chord quality

items.q: Which notes form C major?
items.why: C to E is a major third, and C to G is a perfect fifth.
misconceptions: Mixes up major and minor
Confuses C major with F major
Confuses a triad with a sus chord

items.q: A major and A minor differ in which note or notes?
items.why: Both chords share the same root and the same perfect fifth.
misconceptions: Thinks the fifth sets the quality

Thinks major and minor share no notes

items.q: Which three notes make up a triad?
items.why: A triad stacks a third and a fifth on the root.
misconceptions: Stacks the wrong intervals
Confuses a triad with a sus4 chord
Confuses a triad with a power chord

items.q: Spell D minor.
items.why: D to F is a minor third, and D to A is a perfect fifth.

items.q: Spell G major.
items.why: G to B is a major third, and G to D is a perfect fifth.

lessons.title: The Seven Chords of a Major Key
lessons.objective: Build all seven chords of a major key and name their qualities.
lessons.hook: These seven chords are your palette for writing progressions.
lessons.explain: Diatonic chords are built by stacking every other note of the scale. In C major, stacking from D gives D F A. A major key has seven diatonic triads, one on each scale note, so your guess was right. In a major key, chords on scale degrees 1, 4, and 5 are major: C, F, and G. In a major key, chords on degrees 2, 3, and 6 are minor: Dm, Em, and Am. The chord on degree 7 is diminished: a minor third and a fifth of 6 half steps (B D F).
key_facts: Diatonic chords are built by stacking every other note of the scale.
A major key has seven diatonic triads, one on each scale note.
In a major key, chords on scale degrees 1, 4, and 5 are major.
In a major key, chords on degrees 2, 3, and 6 are minor.
The chord on degree 7 is diminished: a minor third and a fifth of 6 half steps.

predict.q: Using only notes from C major, what chord do you get when you build on D?

angles: Imagine the seven scale notes placed around a circular track. Hop over one note each time and land three times to make a chord. Try it starting on G in C major and measure the gaps yourself.
Check each chord with your thirds knowledge. Count frets from the root to the middle note, then from the root to the top note, and judge the quality from those two counts.

rungs.text: Chord on degree 6 of C major: start on A, skip B, take C, skip D, take E. That gives A C E. A to C is 3 half steps, so the chord is A minor.
Chord on degree 3 of C major: start on E, skip F, take __, skip A, take __. E to G is __ half steps, so the chord is __.
Build the chord on degree 4 of C major and name its quality.

claims: A major key has seven diatonic triads.
Degrees 1, 4, and 5 are major.
Degrees 2, 3, and 6 are minor.
Degree 7 is diminished.
B D F is B diminished.

Counts the octave as a new chord

lessons.title: Roman Numeral Chord Names
lessons.objective: Read and write progressions as Roman numerals.
lessons.hook: Numerals let you move any progression to any key.
lessons.explain: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree, so progressions work in any key. Uppercase numerals mean major chords, like I, IV, V. Lowercase numerals mean minor chords, like ii, iii, vi. A small circle marks a diminished chord, like vii°. The full major-key set is I ii iii IV V vi vii°. In C major, I–vi–IV–V means C–Am–F–G.
key_facts: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree, so progressions work in any key.
Uppercase numerals mean major chords, like I, IV, V.
Lowercase numerals mean minor chords, like ii, iii, vi.
A small circle marks a diminished chord, like vii°.
angles: Think of numerals as seat numbers in a theater. The seat numbers stay the same even when a different audience, or key, fills them. The style of the label also tells you something about the chord.
Take F major (F G A B♭ C D E) and label each chord with its degree number. Decide the letter case from the qualities you built earlier.
claims: Uppercase numerals mean major chords.
Lowercase numerals mean minor chords.
° marks a diminished chord.
In C major, I–vi–IV–V is C–Am–F–G.

items.why: A is degree 6, and the lowercase numeral means minor.
misconceptions: Ignores the lowercase

Confuses vi with IV

items.why: The small circle marks a diminished chord.
misconceptions: Ignores the circle

items.why: The letter case and the circle show each chord's quality.

lessons.title: Finding the Chords in Any Key: G Major
lessons.objective: List the seven chords of any major key.
lessons.hook: Knowing a key's chords tells you which chords will fit your song.
lessons.explain: To find a key's chords, write its scale and apply I ii iii IV V vi vii°. G major's scale is G A B C D E F#. Lay the numeral pattern over it, and the chords of G major are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, and F#dim. That is why songs in G use the open chords G, C, D, Em, and Am so often. In G major, I–IV–V is G–C–D.
key_facts: To find a key's chords, write its scale and apply I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
The chords of G major are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, and F#dim.
In G major, I–IV–V is G–C–D.

lessons.title: Chord Functions: Home, Away, and Tension
lessons.objective: Explain the roles of the tonic, subdominant, and dominant chords.
lessons.hook: Function is what makes a progression feel like it is going somewhere.
lessons.explain: The I chord is the tonic, which feels like home. The IV chord is the subdominant, which moves away from home. The V chord is the dominant, which creates tension that wants to resolve to I. Chords that share notes can share jobs. ii often substitutes for IV, and vi often substitutes for I, because they share two notes. For example, in C major, Am (A C E) shares C and E with C (C E G). If a song in C major ends on G, it feels unfinished.
key_facts: The I chord is the tonic, which feels like home.
The V chord is the dominant, which creates tension that wants to resolve to I.
The IV chord is the subdominant, which moves away from home.
ii often substitutes for IV, and vi often substitutes for I, because they share two notes.

predict.q: A song in C major stops on a G chord. How does it feel?

angles: Think of a story: home, a trip outward, a cliffhanger, then the return. Play D–G–A and stop, then add D, and notice which moment felt like the cliffhanger.
Spell two chords from the same key and circle the notes they have in common. Chords with more notes in common can more easily stand in for each other.
claims: I is the tonic.
IV is the subdominant.
V is the dominant and resolves to I.
vi shares two notes with I.
ii shares two notes with IV.

lessons.title: Common Progressions and Cadences
lessons.objective: Write progressions using proven patterns and cadences.
lessons.hook: These patterns are the starting templates for countless songs.
lessons.explain: I–V–vi–IV is one of the most common pop progressions. In G major it is G–D–Em–C. ii–V–I is the standard way to approach the tonic in jazz and pop, as in Dm–G–C in C major. Moving V to I is called an authentic cadence and sounds final. To write a progression, start on I, move away, build tension with V, and return. Try I–vi–ii–V in G: G–Em–Am–D, then back to G.
key_facts: I–V–vi–IV is one of the most common pop progressions.
ii–V–I is the standard way to approach the tonic in jazz and pop.
Moving V to I is called an authentic cadence and sounds final.
To write a progression, start on I, move away, build tension with V, and return.

predict.q: What is I–V–vi–IV in G major?

angles: Convert a song you already play by ear into numerals. Find its home chord, call it I, and count up the scale to label the rest. Many songs reuse the same loop.
Think of a progression as a round trip. Decide where you leave from, where you wander, and which chord will make the listener lean forward before you arrive back home.

ii–V–I is a standard approach to the tonic.

lessons.title: Relative Minor Keys
lessons.objective: Find a major key's relative minor and write progressions that feel minor.
lessons.hook: The same chords can sound sad or happy depending on which one feels like home.
lessons.explain: Every major key has a relative minor that uses the same notes. The relative minor starts on degree 6 of the major scale. A minor is the relative minor of C major: A B C D E F G. The chords are the same, but home is different. In a minor key, the vi chord of the major key becomes the home chord, i. So Am–F–C–G sounds minor if it keeps landing on Am. Am–F–G–C sounds major once it resolves to C.
key_facts: Every major key has a relative minor that uses the same notes.
The relative minor starts on degree 6 of the major scale.
A minor is the relative minor of C major.
In a minor key, the vi chord of the major key becomes the home chord, i.

predict.q: What is the relative minor of G major?

angles: Think of the same set of rooms with a different front door. The furniture, or notes, stays the same, but where you enter and rest changes the feel. Try F major: count up its scale to the sixth note yourself.
Loop the four chords of a progression and stop on a different chord each time. Notice which stopping point feels most like 'home' and whether that home sounds bright or dark.
claims: Relative major and minor keys share the same notes.
The relative minor starts on degree 6.
A minor is the relative minor of C major.
E minor is the relative minor of G major.

items.q: Find the relative minor of D major and explain how you found it.
items.answer: B minor, because B is degree 6 of D major
accept: Bm, the sixth degree of D major
items.why: The relative minor starts on degree 6.

items.q: In A minor, which chord is the home chord, i?
items.why: The vi of C major becomes i in A minor.
